## Simple explanation

Docker packages an application and many of its dependencies into a
container image. The image can then be run in a more consistent
environment across development, testing, and deployment.

## Technical explanation

Docker uses images as layered, read-only templates and containers as
running instances. Containers share the host operating-system kernel but
isolate processes and resources. They are distinct from virtual machines,
which typically virtualize a complete operating system.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Containers can make model-serving environments reproducible and simplify
deployment. Large models and GPU workloads also require attention to
image size, drivers, hardware access, data mounts, security, and runtime
configuration.

## How it works

A Dockerfile describes how to build an image from a base image, files,
dependencies, and startup configuration. A container runs from that image
with configured resources, environment variables, networking, and
volumes.

## Practical example

A team can package an inference API with its application dependencies in
a Docker image, then run that image in a staging environment before
deploying it to a container platform.

## Common misconceptions

- A container is not a full virtual machine.
- An image does not automatically include model weights or data unless
  explicitly packaged or mounted.
- Containers improve consistency but do not by themselves guarantee
  secure or reproducible builds.
